utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the map is basically the same in these two pieces of work. If you take into account the territories indicated by Moljevic at the time, you have the same map. Tomasevich did not invent this map. He just took a map that had been printed at the time in 1941, that by Moljevic. And Tomasevich is, indeed, of Croat origin, but he is regarded as somebody who is not so negative towards the Chetnik Movement in his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if your answer to Mr. Seselj's objection is that Mr. Tomasevich basically only took again the map by Stevan Moljevic and you say that these are identical maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, nearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are they identical or are they basically the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not notice any differences. If any, then it's a detail only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not been provided with the map by Stevan Moljevic. In the expert report by this witness, we have a map by Jozo Tomasevich. It is a geographic map 7, a component part of the expert report. Madam Dahl has presented us with the same map with comments written by a Serb author obviously many years after the Second World War. It could not have been Stevan Moljevic because Moljevic was arrested by the communists and sentenced to many years' imprisonment, and I think he died in prison. So we have one map that has been identified. Mrs. Dahl has not identified the second one, and we do not have the original one from the journal, Nasput. It has been preserved; there are copies of it. Why didn't she produce it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it appears that in this journal, Nasput, there was this map by Moljevic, and Mr. Seselj is asking why it was not used. Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not able to find this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But the authors who used this map, when they wrote this book on the National Programme of the Ravna Gora Movement are authors, one of whom is a specialist in Serbia of the history of the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you do have the map from Nasput, you can show it to the witness, because he says that he doesn't have it but he trusts those who worked on it, including somebody who was a specialist in the history of the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kosta Nikolic who wrote three volumes on the history of the Ravna Gora Movement and had -- and published other works, some of which were mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, in --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all of these interventions of mine would have been unnecessary if the Prosecutor and the witness had clearly stated what we are talking about. The source of one man is Jozo Tomasevich; the source of the other is Kosta Nikolic, a new author who studied this issue. There is no original map. You see how much time we could have saved if they had clearly stated all this right at the beginning instead of us turning around in a circle and concealing certain facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We got the message. Well, this Moljevic apparently died in detention; and according to Mr. Seselj, he had been arrested by the communists. Did he have any publications? Do you have books with maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was able to find is reproductions of the texts and the map, but this map is not challenged not even by expert historians of the Ravna Gora Movement, including Kosta Nikolic, who's not at all a historian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we have no material document that makes it possible to ascribe the authorship to Mr. Moljevic with certainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but these historians worked on archives, military archives in Belgrade. I just wanted to stress that Kosta Nikolic is a historian who's not at all negative towards the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would seem that Mr. Seselj's objection lacks a good-faith basis that there is some discrepancies in this map in the historical record, and I would ask that he be precluded from interrupting the examination and obfuscating the points that I'm trying to elicit from the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, can you describe how Mr. Moljevic viewed the objective of creating a homogenous Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Moljevic hails from Banja Luka in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and his interest has always been to defend the Serbs from that area. When he suggested that a Greater Serbia be created, a Greater Serbia that would extend to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Dalmatia, up to the north of Sibenik, he wanted this territory to be nationally as homogenous as possible. So he did not want to have a co-habitation or co-existence of Serbs and Croats in that territory because the massacres against the -- because of the massacres against the Serbs in 1941 and 1942 in the territory of the Independent Croat state.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he advocate taking over and ethnically cleansing certain towns?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He indicated a certain number of towns that needed to be taken over and which needed to be captured in Slavonia, which was part of the territory of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you list the towns from which he recommended driving out Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to make another objection. I did not hear the witness say that Moljevic advocated the expulsion of Croats and Muslims from certain towns and territories, and we were supplied here with a copy of Moljevic's text from which we can see that he advocated an exchange of populations. And I think it is clear to anyone that exchange and expulsion is not the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this is a leading question which is put to the expert which are also impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are matters for Mr. Seselj to raise with the witness in cross-examination, and I think that the procedures need to be applied fairly so that my direct examination is not unnecessarily interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, but Mr. Seselj appears to be reproaching you for a leading question which I didn't notice. So could you rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, let's turn to your report at page 53, and I'd like to directly your attention to the Ravna Gora Movement and its policy on ethnic cleansing. In your analysis of Mr. Moljevic's positions, did you form an opinion about whether he took a position on the means by which to accomplish his objective of creating a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: During the war, he mentioned exchanges of population, but also the cleansing of non-Serb elements from territories that should have been taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What territories did he recommend be ethnically cleansed of inhabitants who were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He mentions, in a letter addressed to Dragisa Vasic, the towns of Slavonia of the military border, Karlovac, Knin, and also towns in Herzegovina like Mostar and Metkovic. Actually, being from Banja Luka, Moljevic, while accompanying Draza Mihajlovic, he constantly spoke of the western territories of Serbs, and he insisted with Draza that they defend the interests of the Serbs in these regions, because these populations were not sufficiently supported during the inter-war period. And that is why the town he mentions are towns that were within the Banovina or Croatia -- of Croatia or part of the Independent State of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 53, I'm going to read, and you say: "According to Moljevic, it was a question of applying the policy of fait accompli. The mapped-out territory had to be taken over, in the first place," such and such towns, "and to proceed with cleansing." And, in footnote 106, this was contained in a letter addressed to Dragisa Vasic, and this letter was published in a work published by Dedijer and Miletic. So this document which could have been important, why didn't you include it in your report, this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it is a letter. It is part of a private correspondence, if you like, between two members of the movement. So it is not of the same nature as a brochure of 1941, for example, when reference is made to homogenous Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he speaks of cleansing in private correspondence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But it reflects the ideas that had been previously formulated, and I referred to this earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this letter exists; it is in this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have quoted most of the works that refer to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a brief objection. The author should now -- or the author of this expert report should state clearly that the original source of this document is a collection of documents and data of the National Liberation War of the Peoples of Yugoslavia, volume 14, book 1. He states this in footnote 106. That is the first source, and that collection is full of forged documents which the communists produced for political and ideological reasons. Everything else uncritically taken over by individual authors is not relevant for us here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a matter for cross-examination, and Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- should be asked to bring forward the evidence he is referring to, rather than casting aspersions on documents without proof.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, did the Ravna Gora Movement issue a programme that concerned the radical cleansing of towns to remove non-Serb elements?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, this happened. These are not actions that one found between 1941 and 1944. But it is true that specifically in 1942 in the region of Foca in Bosnia, Eastern Bosnia, and also in January and February 1943, again in Eastern Bosnia and also in Sandzak, units under the command of Djurisic, who was a leader of the Yugoslav Army in the homeland, these units did massacre civilian populations. So these were reprisals at the time following attacks suffered by the Chetniks. But when we see the number of victims in each of these -- on each of these sides, we see that there were very few victims on the Chetnik side, a certain number of military victims among the Muslims who were involved in these operations, but above all there were women and children and the elderly who were killed in large numbers. So historians asked themselves the question whether this was purely an operation in reprisal, or was there a link between the idea of creating a homogenous Greater Serbia and these events. And we note that in certain documents mention is made of the regulation of the Muslim question and the cleansing of Muslims from certain territories, and one can therefore conclude that this was part of the motivation behind these events with a view to reducing the number of Muslims in the areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djurisic make reports on the killings by his units?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, to several reports to the command, to the military command, of the Ravna Gora Movement, in which he described the operations conducted at the time and especially in January and February 1943.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was the military command at the time that Mr. Djurisic reported to?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He reported to Draza Mihajlovic, who was the supreme commander of the Ravna Gora Movement and at the same time the Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, I believe that your report at pages 55 and 56 reproduces two reports from 1943 by Mr. Djurisic to Draza Mihajlovic. Can you summarize the first report that he made with regard to the number of villages, the casualties of Muslims versus the casualties of the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He gives a list of Muslim villages that were completely destroyed, a total of 33 villages. He speaks of 400 Muslim combatants that were killed and about 1.000 women and children killed, and the victims on the Chetnik side were 14 killed and 26 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does he indicate whether the attack was carried out as planned?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He says, at the beginning of the document, that the operation was conducted exactly as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he report what happened to the villages after the attack?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He indicates that they were burnt down, that the villages were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Commander Djurisic send in a further report to Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: In other operations of the 13th of February, 1943, he states or he describes the operations in the way they were conducted and he provides the casualty lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the two reports, I am astonished by the figures. The first report of the 10th of January, 400 Muslim fighters; second report, number of Muslim combatants, 1.200, if the figure 1.200 is correct. So there was fighting between the two sides and these combats resulted in losses among Djurisic's troops amounting to 22 killed and 32 wounded. So the Muslims in all these villages, 33 villages, defended themselves. There must have been armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Clearly, there was resistance. If there is an attack, there is some resistance. But when we look at the number of victims on the Chetnik side, we notice that either the attack was very speedy and the Muslim armed men didn't have time to respond. There might have been the surprise effect. Or if on the Chetnik side there were more soldiers, maybe that explains the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these two documents apparently of military origin, as they are combat reports, a Judge asks himself two questions. First: Was there fighting, armed conflict, followed by executions; or was there no conflict, everybody was taken prisoner and executed? You did not focus on these operations. You simply referred to two documents addressed by Djurisic to his Chief of Staff Milanovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't go into the details. But in view of the reports, I can only conclude that the combat didn't last long if there were any at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of the second report, which is reproduced on your report, page 56, does Commander Djurisic indicate whether the enemy offered resistance?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is the report of 13 February 1943, and in the English translation there, it's the third full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He says, in fact, that the resistance of the enemy was weak from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is there any indication of whether the attack was carried out in conformity with the orders and commands?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is clearly stated, in the -- as in the first report, that the operations were carried out in conformity with the orders and commands. The attack started as planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you look at the middle of the report with the sentence beginning: "During the operation, the Muslim population," and can you read that out, please, continuing through the list of casualties.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: "During the operation, the Muslim population was completely destroyed, irrespective of sex and age."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And the next line.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: "Casualties: We had 22 dead, two of whom were killed by accident, and 32 wounded."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And "Among the Muslims ..."

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: "Among the Muslims: 1.200 fighters and 8.000 women, elderly people, and children."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you kindly read the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: "At the outset of the operation, the Muslims took flight towards Metaljka, Cajnice, and the river Drina. Part of the population took shelter in Metaljka. There are an estimated 2.000 refugees in Cajnice, some of whom were able to get away before our units had blocked off possible escape routes in this sector. The rest of the population was completely destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the estimate of the total number of victims in the operations against the Muslims in January and February 1943?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Roughly 10.000, approximately 10.000, the number of victims during these operations of January and February 1943.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How about in Montenegro between 1942 and mid-1943?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: The estimate is about 3.000 victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were divisions of the Ravna Gora Movement active at this time-period in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: They were active in the Independent State of Croatia, which at the time included the state of Croatia proper and part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the region of Krajina, in Lika and the north of Dalmatia and also in the Bosnian part of Krajina, there were operations by Chetnik units of the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who commanded the Chetnik units in that region?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Djujic, in one of the regions, he was the leader. He was in command; he was the military leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, your report covers an attack by Chetnik forces of Croatian villages in 1942 and 1943. Can you focus on the Dinara operation in October 1942? Can you tell me what forces commanded by Commander Djujic did in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, Momcilo Djujic was at the head of the Dinara Chetnik division and were inside the Croatian independent state. There were numerous cases of combat between the various parties. There were fights between either the Chetniks and Croatian Ustasha, and similarly between the Chetniks and the communist partisans. So it depended on the incursions of the various parties into the territory. And depending on these incursions, there were Chetnik responses; and in course of certain operations, civilians were affected.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At the end of the war, what happened with Commander Djujic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Djujic managed to escape, initially to Slovenia and then to Italy. Later on, in the 1950s, he immigrated to the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did he do in the United States with regard to the Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He founded the Serbian Chetnik of Ravna Gora. In some way, he nurtured this memory of the movement of the combatants. There were commemorative events that were held regularly and every year. This movement had assemblies in the course of those years. Well, it was a movement of a veterans, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why wasn't he extradited from the US? You mentioned something in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several requests for extradition. I don't know of the exact reason for which he wasn't extradited, but I think it was an isolated case because there were other war criminals. It wasn't an isolated case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there was a demand for extradition, I -- well, in the 1990s in Yugoslavia, there must have been an investigating judge who was dealing with everything that had happened in the territory and who must have initiated this. Have you looked into this matter or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At the beginning of this morning, you mentioned that Momcilo Djujic had proclaimed Dr. Seselj a Chetnik Vojvoda. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: End of June, 1989. At the time, Vojislav Seselj went to the US and held a number of conferences there for the Serbs from the US and for former Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your conclusion, there seems to be something that's incoherent in my opinion. You say, in June 1989, Djujic made Seselj a Vojvoda, and then you continue and you say: "So there is a direct link between the Chetnik Movement from the Second World War and the political movement founded by Vojislav Seselj in 1990. Seselj was made a Vojvoda in 1989. How do you get to 1990 in the same sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're dealing with June 1989 here, and then Vojislav Seselj established a party in January 1990. This was the Libertas Movement, the Freedom Movement in Serb; and in June 1990, he created the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The Chetnik Movement of Ravna Gora led by Momcilo Djujic believed that the movement of Chetniks created in Serbia was, in fact, part of his own movement. So he was, in fact, responsible for the movement in the free world and the US in this case, and Mr. Seselj was responsible for the movement in the homeland, in the home country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when Mr. Seselj was made a Vojvoda, at the time he wasn't at the head of that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In fact, he wasn't at the head of a party; he wasn't the leader of a party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was a personal appointment or nomination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first free elections took place in spring 1990, so multi-party -- the multi-party system hadn't been recognised at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask what time we'll be taking the next break, so I can plan my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should be having a break at 11.50, so we have another 20 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, perhaps there's been an interpretation error, but I heard the witness say that the first multi-party elections were held in spring 1990. That's what I heard; that's how it was interpreted. I don't know whether that's correct, but perhaps we could try and clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, the multi-party elections, when were they held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April 1990 in Croatia; and then in Slovenia; in Serbia, it was in December 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the multi-party elections, April 1990 in Croatia and Slovenia and December 1990 in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In preparation of your report, did you undertake a study of the writings and development of the political ideology of Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When did Dr. Seselj begin taking part in political or intellectual debates?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that he started taking part in such debates, or rather, he started publishing in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In 1981.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were articles in the Belgrade press in which he put into question a certain number -- or he cast out a certain number of Bosnian Muslim intellectuals. He accused them of defending Islamist or pan-Islamist positions at the time. He also denounced Branko Milesa's case of plagiarism. He was a leader of the communist party in Bosnia. In Sarajevo, he had drafted a thesis for his post-graduate studies, and he had copied certain passages. He had plagiarised certain passages from authors who were leaders at the time. So, when these articles were published, after they were published, there were numerous debates that communist bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina reacted, in particular they reacted strongly in Sarajevo, and they excluded Vojislav Seselj from the Yugoslav League of Communists in December 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj formulate opinions about the Serbian national question at that time?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: In 1981, not immediately. It was a little later, after the history that concern -- after the story that concerns the journalist's investigation. It had to do with a communist newspaper, Bogavac. He was involved in an investigation called, What To Do, and this was within the political and economic crisis in Yugoslavia. He wanted to interrogate some intellectuals to see what their opinions were on the crisis that the country was going through. Vojislav Seselj wanted to participate in this project and drafted an article in which he said what his vision was of how the Yugoslav Federation should be reorganized. This text was seized by the security forces, by the police; and on the basis of this document which was never published, he was condemned to eight years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How long did he serve?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: One year and ten months. In this document, he suggests that the Yugoslav Federation be reorganized into four federal units; whereas, the country was composed of six such units. And he suggested that the country's federal units should be Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to page 69 in your report, where I believe you quote some materials published by Dr. Seselj on this matter.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an extract from the document that was subsequently published in one of Mr. Seselj's books.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: It was published in "Democracy and Dogma" in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What were Mr. Seselj's views on the redrawing of borders between Serbia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He, in fact, suggested a new territorial border between Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What would he use to draw the line?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: That in particular --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment to make. Mr. President, I believe that the witness should express his opinion now because he said my book "Democracy and Dogma" was published in 1991. Was that the first edition or a subsequent edition? Could we say when my book"Democracy and Dogma" was published for the first time. This is very important for this examination, because if we leave it at 1991, the matters will be confused. Could the witness please say when my book"Democracy and Dogma" was published for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Democracy and Dogma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used the 1991 version, but there must have been a prior version that must have been banned at the end of the 1980s, 1988 or 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was written a few years earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a few years earlier, not more than that, and it appeared at a subsequent date after the change of the political regime, after the process of democracy had started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj will tell us, in the course of the cross-examination, when exactly he published "Dogma and Democracy." Ms. Dahl, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like to return to the question that Mr. Seselj's objection interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: On what basis did Mr. Seselj propose redrawing the borders between Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, he suggested a new delimitation of the border based on the following principle: He said there were just as many Croats in Serbia as there were Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So was he going to use population figures to establish a new border?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the census was quite precise, and it was possible to know how the various nationalities were represented in each part of Yugoslavia. So that was a possible source. So there was information, detailed information, on how the various nations or nationalities were represented in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that in the text that was published, he says that the national Serbo-Croat question would be finally dealt with on the basis of humanistic and democratic principles and on the basis of an agreement. Is that what he wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, were there any repercussions when this was published? Did this affect the political opinions at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the book appeared, is that what you mean? Well, we're taking into consideration the 1991 version, not the first version in this case, not the first version that was banned. And at the time Yugoslavia was breaking up, that was the context. So these statements have a different scope because of the time reference was made to reorganizing the Yugoslav Federation, and there was a series of negotiations between the leaders of the various republics, the purpose of which was to see whether Yugoslavia should be transformed into a confederation or to a federation, should a more centralist system be introduced, or should the republics be accorded more autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His proposition, his suggestion, seems to be twofold. Initially, he seems to want to maintain or to keep Croats in Serbia and Serbs in Croatia. That's the main principle; and then on the basis of the census, one would delimit the border, one would trace the border. You have studied the issue. Was this technically feasible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in fact, in Serbia such as in -- had been envisaged, Serbia would have included Bosnia and Herzegovina. So one would have had to count the number of Croats in that republic, since it would have become part of federal Serbia and one would have had to count the number of Croats in Serbia and one would have had to compare that number with the number of Serbs living in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the text that you must have read on numerous occasions, did it involve moving the population because one has the impression that these people didn't move. Their existence has been recognised but they don't move; it's the borders that are to move. Am I mistaken or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Croatia, about 12 per cent of the population was Serbian. There were about 4.700.000 Croats. If you count the number of Serbs -- I apologise, the number of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they represented 22 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given such figures, do such figures imply the status quo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they're not comparable, if they're not identical, well, we can't proceed then. One can't proceed. I can't make the calculation. I can't remember the exact census figures for 1981, but one should do the calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main question on the basis of this text is: Would the consequence be moving the population and everything that that implies, or was this just a matter of drawing a conclusion? Was this a matter of stating that there were ethnic minorities and these ethnic minorities were to remain where they were? And one would then trace the borders on the basis of the census statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the text isn't explicit enough. One can't really see the idea of moving the population in the text, but I don't have all the figures. I know that there were about 178.000 Croats in Serbia, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be added to the number, we should compare it with the number of Serbs, and we should see whether there was a balance or an imbalance between the two sets of figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this text which comes from the end of the 1980s --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This text was drafted in 1983 or 1984. It was taken from Vojislav Seselj's apartment in the spring 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was a time when Seselj -- Mr. Seselj was speaking about administrative borders, not international ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was speaking about internal borders between the various republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. So perhaps we should also look at the question of not moving the population, within that context, within the context of internal administrative borders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last question before the break: In your report, did you include this idea of administrative borders in the former Yugoslavia, as my colleague has put it; and in this idea of borders, did you refer to how they could have -- these borders could have had political connotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, the reference is only made to the territories on the basis of the boundaries of the borders of republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. At the time, there are internal administrative boundaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but at the time Yugoslavia was recognised internationally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's ten to 12.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before the break, we were discussing the manuscript entitled: "Answers to an Interview: What is to be done?" Can you describe why the proposal to organize the Yugoslav Federation into four republics and a revision of the border between Serbia and Croatia would be considered counter-revolutionary activities against the social order?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: At the time Yugoslavia was made up of six republics, so this is questioning the federal structure that was created during World War II at the initiative of the communist partisans. This order was supposed to settle the national question in all of Yugoslavia. It was not conceivable at the time to see a restructuring of this Federation into four republics. Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been part of Serbia then. This was regarded as a nationalist position. Nationalism at the time was repressed in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj take part in the debates on constitutional changes in the Republic of Serbia in 1988?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. At the time there were amendments that were proposed, constitutional reform had been proposed in Serbia. It, in particular, dealt with the definition of the autonomous provinces within Serbia. Serbia was the only republic that had two autonomous provinces; in the north it was Vojvodina, and the south it was Kosovo. These two autonomous provinces were recognised as federal units and fully so. So this raised a problem for Serbia because the central power in Serbia could not intervene in the affairs of these two autonomous provinces. At the time Slobodan Milosevic had taken control of the political apparatus. He was the main leader in Serbia, and there was an initiative to change the constitution. This reform aimed at reducing the prerogatives of the autonomous provinces. This led to many debates in numerous organizations, the Writers' Union, the Association of Researchers at the time, and Vojislav Seselj did take part in such debates.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask that a map of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia be displayed. It's 65 ter number 07005, and it's in the map book at map number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Dahl, could you kindly repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at this map, can you explain to the Chamber the republics and which were the autonomous units or the autonomous provinces? I think there's an electronic pen that you can use that will display.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Here is, in the north, the autonomous province of Vojvodina; and in the south, that of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you indicate the other republics.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Starting from the north, you have the Republic of Slovenia; that of Croatia; Bosnia and Herzegovina; Serbia, with the two autonomous provinces; the Republic of Montenegro; and that of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can I have the map marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P143.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like the whole map marked not just his indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl, my fellow Judge is wondering that, and me, too, why marked for identification? Why not give it a definitive number. There's no challenge to that. It was authenticated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I was following the practice from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the annotated map will be MFI P143 and the unannotated will be MFI P -- will be Exhibit P144.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In 1988, when Mr. Seselj proposed restructuring the Federation, did he propose the same ideas as previously with regard to the number of republics or federal units?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: No, he went back. He changed his previous position. He thought that Yugoslavia had to be restructured into three federal units: Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia. Compared to the previous proposal, the Republic of Macedonia would disappear and would become part of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What reasons did Dr. Seselj express for limiting the number of federal units to three?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Actually, Macedonia is regarded by many Serbs as being south or southern Serbia. Macedonians are, in fact, regarded as being Serbs; therefore, it is to be found in most of the Greater Serbian projects as a former territory of the medieval Serbia anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Dr. Seselj express a view on the Macedonian or Muslim nations?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He believes that the Macedonian nation is an artificial one created by the communist regime in Yugoslavia. This goes for the Muslim nation which was recognised in 1968. He believes, too, that it is an artificial nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did Mr. Seselj's views align with the conceptual framework of the first Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: If you look at the proposal he made in late 1980s for a federal Yugoslavia in three units, we're going back to the first framework of the first Yugoslavia. In the first Yugoslavia, there was a Yugoslav nation with three tribes: The Slovenes, the Croats, and the Serbs. And other nations were not recognised at the time. In proposing to restructure the Yugoslav Federation into three republics with the Slovenes, the Croats, and the Serbs, we go back to the concept that was prevalent between the two wars.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask the registrar to take the map down because we're finished with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the reason that Dr. Seselj went to the United States in 1989?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He got in touch with the Serbian Chetniks of the -- among the migrants, the Serbian Ravna Gora headed by Momcilo Djujic; and, in 1989, he went to give lectures and conferences held -- organized throughout the country. And, during these conferences, he's going to expound his political programme for the future of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to page 73 of your report, where you excerpt Dr. Seselj's national programme as he articulated it in 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Before we deal with this, let me go back to what you just said. So Mr. Seselj went to the United States and gave a series of lectures. Did you ask yourself what setting it was in? Was he there as a tourist, as a green card resident? Because it appears he stayed there for quite some time. Based on that, did he go with the agreement of the Americans? Because you can't just go to the American territory and hold lectures for months on end without enjoying some kind of status from the point of view of immigration. Did you look into this matter? Because if I connect his visit with the fact that the Americans were against the extradition of the one who had appointed him a Vojvod, we are entitled to raise quite a number of issues. Did you look into it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had been convicted so he didn't have a passport; that was banned. And when he went to the United States, he got a passport again. At the time, Vojislav Seselj was regarded as a dissent of the communist rule, and he was supported by numerous human rights organizations, including in the United States. So he had this I image of being an opponent to his communist regime of being a defender of human rights. So he was supported by organization in favour of free expression in Yugoslavia and more specifically in Serbia, but he was also supported by numerous organizations in Europe, as in the United States. So it's not surprising that the United States let him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that he enjoyed the same status as Solzhenitsyn [Realtime transcript missing word "Solzhenitsyn"]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that he was regarded as a dissident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the time he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the interpreter does not know Solzhenitsyn. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is the court reporter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you please read the excerpt you have drawn from Dr. Seselj's book, and I am referring to the paragraph at page 73.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is at e-court 02802A.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the paragraph that begins: "We Serbs in Yugoslavia must define our national goals ..."

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm reading it. "We Serbs in Yugoslavia must define our national goals, our national programme, and the borders of our state, while allowing our supposed northern brothers, the Croats and the Slovenes, can express themselves in full freedom whether they want to live in such a state or not. The Serbian people is not a priori opposed to the existence of Yugoslavia. I'm deeply convinced that the Serbian people is in favour of the existence of Yugoslavia, but it does not want Yugoslavia at any price. "It only wants a Yugoslavia whose frontiers would respect the borders of Serbian statehood, as guaranteed by the Treaty of London. Therefore, should a federal Yugoslavia remain in existence, the Serbian federal unit should comprise within its borders not only the current territory of Serbia and the current provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija, but Macedonia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Lika, Banija, Kordun, Eastern Slavonia, and Baranja. "These borders are not guaranteed by the Treaty of London but were drawn by Ante Pavelic during World War II. He drew them with Serbian graves, Serbian mass burials, Serbian suffering, camps, massacre sites, and pits, and I think that the Serbian people must on no account allow a single Serbian mass grave to remain outside the borders of the Serbian state."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The interpreter several times orally, and now in the written text, too, of the expert report, there's mention of the Slovenes. It should say "Slovenians." There's an enormous difference between Slovenes and Slovenians. Slovenes or Slavs is the general concept applied to all Slav people, Serbs, Russians, Czechs, and all others. And Slovenians are a small Slav people. So the interpreters orally make the same mistake often, and I think it is important to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But with regard to the text that you wrote into your national programme, where's the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have received as an expert report was probably translated from the French; and in the third line, it says: "To Croats and Slovenes," and it should say "Croats and Slovenians." There's an enormous difference between Slavs and Slovenians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in the French version, it is the Croats and the Slovenes; but, apparently, in the English translation that Mr. Seselj has in his language, it was misinterpreted. So having specified that, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you draw from Dr. Seselj's text for your research?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used all the works that he has written, also the interviews he granted to various media, and there are numerous compilations of those statements and interviews. So there is a host of documents and very important texts to follow the evolution of the ideas of Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In what language did you study Dr. Seselj's writings?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Directly in Serbian, in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text, which is an important one, there are two matters which I wish to refer to. The first element is the Treaty of London, because this text refers to the Treaty of London regarding the frontiers emanating from the Treaty of London. And the second highlight of this text are all these symmetries of massacred Serbs that were victimised in the Second World War, and there is a demand on the part of the author of the text that those Serbs who are buried there should be buried in -- within the boundaries of a Serbian state. The Treaty of London, what is it exactly for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Treaty of London concluded on the 26th of April, 1915. It was a text among the forces of the Entente: France, Great Britain, and Russia; and to have Italy join against the central powers, that is, Austro-Hungary and Germany --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I may interject briefly and ask the registrar to bring up map number 9, which illustrates the Treaty of London, I think it may make the testimony visible in terms of the territorial negotiations. It's at page 109 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a map 9 that corresponds to the Treaty of London. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to have Italy join in the war, it was necessary to satisfy its national aspirations and to grant it a certain number of territories along the Adriatic coast on the Yugoslav side. So the Treaty of London will define parts of the literal that will belong to each of the countries of the region. Therefore, the treaty in itself has nothing to do with the concept of the Greater Serbia. It was not a question of creating a Greater Serbia. Serbia itself was not a party to the negotiations, and it was informed post festum, after the event. But, nevertheless, there was the idea of granting to Serbia Bosnia-Herzegovina. Actually, if the Allies of the Entente wanted to give Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia, it was because the Serbs were asked to cede a good part of Macedonia. So this was a matter of territorial compensation, because at the same time since the autumn of 1914, the forces of the Entente were endeavouring to persuade the Bulgarians and the Romanians to join the conflict against the central forces. I think the question of the distribution of the coast is very important, if I can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm looking at the wrong screen. It is enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, Serbia was granted a part of the literal going from Ploca in Serbo-Croatia and the entire territory south of that cape that is north of Split up to ten kilometres south of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The translation is wrong again. I don't know what the witness has said in the original, but the interpreter is telling me that it is the territory south of Ploca. Maybe the interpreters don't know anything, but the witness should know. It is the Palanka cape above Split. Ploca and Palanka is not the same. Ploca is far further to the south of Split.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Palanka is not a village; it is just a promontory. So the term used by Western diplomacy was Palanka. So south of Palanka was given to Serbia; further to the north, the territory south of Karlobag. All of this was returned to Italy. Then the area of Volusko close to Opatija up to south of Karlobag was given to Croatia, and the whole of Istria to Italy. So the Treaty of London actually divides the literal, but it doesn't concern itself with the borders inland, only with the coast, part of which is given to Serbia; and, therefore, one could conclude that the territory behind the coast is also granted to Serbia, in this case Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we give this map a number, an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Dahl.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second issue, regarding the Serb tombs, should it be inferred from this text that there would be Serbs, for instance, those living in Romania who were killed during the Second World War, is this a requirement regarding those territories based on Serb cemeteries? How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This defines territories on the basis of the locations of the massacres, and it mainly concerns territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, for you, what is indicated here refers to territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that clarification. Madam Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does the negotiations concerning the Treaty of London define any inland boundaries?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: At the time, no. It was later in the months that followed, in June, July, and August in 1915, the forces of the Entente are going to propose territorial compensation to Serbia in view of the fact that Serbia had to cede territory to other countries. But this policy of territorial compensation had nothing to do with the Treaty of London.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: For example, there was a question of granting the region of Banat to Romania; the Serb government refused this suggestion. And to the extent that the support, the military support of Serbia, was required, a region of Slavonia, a part of Slavonia, was granted to Serbia. So this was all part of the logic of territorial compensation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When you compare and contrast the borders of Dr. Seselj's national programme and the claims that he makes based on the Treaty of London with the actual borders ...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And if we could bring back the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: ... can you indicate --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Actually, if we start from the town of Karlobag, which is a small town of some 1.000 inhabitants on the Adriatic coast.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Could you illustrate, please.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: If we take the town of Karlobag, if I can find it, as a point of departure, it is in the zone, the coastal zone, that was to be given to Croatia. It was granted to Serbia, as I have already indicated, starting from the promontory of Palanka. And then if we go from Karlobag to Ogulin, which is further to the north, and then Virovitica, these were not taken into consideration by the Treaty of London. They were not defined by that treaty. There's even a part in the area of Sibenik, the town of Zadar; including the town of Knin, that is the hinterland of Zadar which is an important town for the Serb Krajina. According to the Treaty of London, this belonged to Italy. These were territories that were inhabited to a large extent by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: So there was a kind of distortion between what emanated from the Treaty of London, the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica, there was a distortion of the Treaty of London as that line was not defined by that treaty.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: A distortion by whom?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: By Vojislav Seselj, who is claiming that that was the western border of Serbia. It does not correspond to historical data of the Treaty of London of 1915.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand well, that when Mr. Seselj talks of Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica, this does not correspond to the Treaty of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all. The Treaty of London dealt with the coast and the area apart, north of Zadar up to the delta of the Neretva, the mouth of the Neretva. As further to the north, Karlovac-Virovitica, this was certainly not defined by the Treaty of London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we give this map a number, please. For the needs of the transcript, for the previous map, it was not recorded, P145.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And this map, the second annotation, will be Exhibit P146.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's bring up a clean copy of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to avoid any confusion, I think it is important for me to intervene whenever there is some confusion. The witness quoted part of my speech in the United States; and if you remember well, all the -- it was stated that these borders were not guaranteed by the Treaty of London. They were marked by Ante Pavelic during the Second World War. So there's no need to make any confusion between the Treaty of London and my concept of these borders.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stated this explicitly; and if there is not cleared up, there is some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a matter for cross-examination, and I would like to proceed to my next point.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's -- if you would with the pen, would you outline the treaty boundaries for Serbia on map number 9.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: You mean the coast, the literal?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, the area that would result in Serbia under the treaty.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And if there's a geographic determination you can make of the rest of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, on page 75, you've quoted Dr. Seselj in his book, "Politics as a Challenge of Conscience," and I'm going to read out the claim that you've excerpt --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have another objection. The witness started to draw the border of the rest of Serbia. Mrs. Dahl did not allow him to finish that drawing, and I would like to see it. If the screen is switched off, I can't see what he has drawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want the document, the map, to stay on the screen and the drawing to be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, will you please finish tracing the line of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can suppose that this part, too, was intended for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll give this a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another request, Your Honour, for this to be printed out for me, so that I can cross-examine the witness on the basis of it and I need it, the drawing made by the witness at the end, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, will you please give a copy to Mr. Seselj, but first a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit Number P147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you well, this is not the border emanating from the Treaty of London because you said the Treaty of London only dealt with the borders along the coast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when a part of the coast is given to Serbia, this implies that Bosnia-Herzegovina was also given to Serbia. And, at the time, these territories were suggested to Serbia to compensate the loss of territory of Macedonia because Serbia would lose a part of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you could perhaps say that this was a consequence of the Treaty of London, but this was not part of the treaty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. The Treaty of London did not deal with borders inland.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to read to you an excerpt that you've quoted Dr. Seselj on regarding the boundaries of the Serbian state that he considered guaranteed by this treaty. Would you with your pen and in different colour indicate this boundary of the Serbian federal unit as Dr. Seselj articulated. So he would -- he says: "The boundaries of the Serbian state guaranteed by the 1915 Treaty of London are the only acceptable boundaries of the Serbian federal unit. This means that Serbia shall encompass Serbia proper, Vojvodina, Kosovo and Metohija, Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, Banija, Eastern Slavonia, and Baranja."

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a little difficult, this exercise, because I don't have all the information I need. I don't have the entire map. So to have the -- to draw the line, I'm not sure where everything is located. I don't have all the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, this exercise appears to be a difficult one because he can't do it with this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could take Karlobag, go up to Ogulin, Karlovac, so that's the western border there suggested by Vojislav Seselj. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, see if I can simplify the question of maps. Let's turn to the last map in your report, map number 10, and I ask you if you can tell me what this is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you should warn the witness that his border encompasses Zagreb given the way that he has traced the delimitation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't have the information to draw the line. I did it roughly, but in any event Zagreb is not included in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have that in the transcript now. Let's have a look at the other map.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what map number 10 is?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the territory of Greater Serbia suggested by the Chetnik Serbian Movement. This was published in the journal, Velika Srbija, Greater Serbia. It's this movement's journal. The territory depicted in the map includes Macedonia, which is called southern Serbia here; Kosovo is called old Serbia; Serbia is, well, you have Vojvodina, you have Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Dalmatia; part of the military border area and of the territory of the Republic of Croatia of the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the date of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1st of August, 1990. The Chetnik Serb -- the Serbian Chetnik Movement was established in June 1990, so this is issue number 2 of the journal that appeared a month earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the coast, the London treaty wasn't taken into consideration at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, if you have a look at the zone that goes to the Serb, it starts here at Palanka; at Palanka cape to the north of Split, that is to say west of Trogir; and an area that was given to Serbia starts ten kilometres to the south of Dubrovnik. It's this area here, up to Karlobag that goes to Italy. Between Palanka and Karlobag, this area goes to Italy; and above in April, the area went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the map that was published, this was given to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was Dr. Seselj's relationship to the Serbian Chetnik Movement in August 1990 when this magazine was published?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give this document a number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit Number P148.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was Dr. Seselj's relationship to the Serbian Chetnik Movement at the time this publication was issued in August 1990?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: He was the president, the leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask Your Honour what time we're concluding today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today we will be concluding at 1.15, so you have another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is the programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: The main objective of the Serbian Chetnik Movement is the creation of a Greater Serbia, which would include, in addition to Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dubrovnik, and then territory in Croatia, Lika, Kordun, Banija, Slavonia, the Baranja territory. So that's the main issue, the main objective in the party's programme. In addition, as part of this programme, one also finds the desire to establish a democratic order in Serbia, the rule of law, a market economy, the development of Catholicism [as interpreted] in Serbia. These elements also form part of the programme. The programme also has detailed plans for regulating the Albanian question in Kosovo, because well, the programme has a number of elements that say that there is a course one should follow in order to deal with the Albanian issue, and this course is mentioned. The course of action suggested is the expulsion of 360.000 Albanians who settled in Kosovo during the Second World War. A state of war should also be declared in the province of Kosovo; a buffer zone at the border should be created, a buffer zone in which there would be no Albanians in order to make sure that the border with Albania was secure.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you reprint the programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in your report?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those would be the essential issues, essential points, that were mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And those appear at your report at pages 81 and 82?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: I made reference to the issues that concern the national Serbian question, and I didn't mention all the other elements that have to do with the establishment of democracy and market economy. I didn't mention things that don't directly concern the Serbian national question and tracing the borders.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at what is in your binder as document 83. It's been previously marked for identification as P27. Looking at paragraph number 1, can you read to yourself the borders of the Serbian federal unit that are part of the platform and tell me or tell the Chamber whether that is the same borderline illustrated on the Velika Srbija issue we just saw.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, the map of Greater Serbia results from this point of the programme, so we have the map that shows what the objectives were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How does this political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement relate to the intellectual movements of the 1930s?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And can I ask for an interpreter's question. I think the reference was to the word "capitalism," and it was translated as "Catholicism" at 94, 20.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can confirm that the witness mentioned "capitalism" and not "Catholicism."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Going back to the question: How does the political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement relate to the intellectual movements of the 1930s, specifically with regard to the Serbian national question?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: At the end of the 1930s, the Serbian cultural centre wanted to establish a Serbian entity that would include most of the territory mentioned. A lot of the territory in Croatia is under item 1 of the programme and much of this territory was in the Croatian Banovina. This was a Croatian entity created in 1939 within Yugoslavia. So the cultural -- the Serbian cultural movement wanted the borders of this Croatian entity revised. They thought that a certain number of municipalities were inhabited by Serbs who were in the majority, and they didn't think it was normal for them to be located within the borders of the Croatian entity. So the borders suggested by these two organizations are different, but the objective was the same in any event. They wanted to trace the limits of Serbian entity within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who were the main intellectuals of the Serbian Cultural Club?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: There was the president, Slobodan Jovanovic, who was a very respected lawyer. He was the head of the Yugoslav government in exile during the Second World War. There was also Dragisa Vasic who was the vice-president. He was the chief editor of the Serbian club's journal, Srpski Glas. His name was Dragisa Vasic, and he became part of the Ravna Gora Movement subsequently. He was one of the main leaders of that movement. There was also Stevan Moljevic, he was also a member of this organization; and at the time, he was a lawyer in Banja Luka and was much interested in Serbian national question, in particular after the Banovina in Croatia had been established. This was in August 1939.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the Serbian Cultural Club in the late 1930s organize lectures regarding methods to resolve the Serbian national question?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, at the time, yes. Even before the Croatian entity was established in 1939. In 1937, there were conferences organized on the Serbian national question and on the question of the nationalisation of certain territories where the -- where there was a minority. That was the case in Kosovo and Vojvodina, and these intellectuals who held these conferences often mentioned moving the population and population exchanges as a means of dealing with the issue. Vasic Cubrilovic held a conference on Kosovo, and the idea was to forcibly expel people within Yugoslavia and outside Yugoslavia. There was also Djoko Perin who presented arguments on the nationalisation of Vojvodina and Kosovo, and he was particularly interested in Vojvodina. There was various sketches, various scenarios, the purpose of which was to ensure that the Serbs would be in the majority in Vojvodina, because at the time that wasn't the case. There was a population -- a general population of over 300.000. There were Hungarians, too. So, in each case, the idea was to proceed with population [Realtime transcript read in error "proposition"] exchanges or to encourage or compel national minorities to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement is something I'd like to ask you about. When we have a look at the situation in paragraph 1, I'm struck by the following. Reference is made to Serbian territory. Everything else appears to me to be a reaction to the communist regime and to what Tito had done, except for at the end where mention is made of the expulsion of Albanian -- of Albanian immigrants. So, as far as this political programme is concerned, what was its main objective in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, in 1990, there were troubles in Croatia, and one of the main activities of the Serbian Chetnik Movement was to ensure its own promotion in Serbia because elections were about to be held towards the end of the year; but in addition to that, it was also to organize sending Serbian volunteers to Croatia in order to defend local Serbian populations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this mentioned in the platform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I can see. Why is it not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main objective is mentioned, but the means to achieve it are not detailed, are not developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We still have a few minutes, four exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me ask for a correction to the interpretation. At 97:24, the witness spoke to "population" exchanges; it was translated as "proposition" exchanges.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters explain that this is the LiveNote which is a very transitional system to transcribe and the final version is verified later on; that applied to previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the time may have come to finish for today. You can continue tomorrow, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] You're reminded that you're not supposed to have any contacts with the Prosecutor. As you know, we're sitting in the morning; this means that we're going to resume and reconvene tomorrow at 8.30. With regard to your time, Ms. Dahl, the registrar has told me that you had used one hour and 35 to 40 minutes. I'm not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to let you know that, during the break, my staff retrieved from the materials provided to us by Mr. Tomic the original Serbian reprints of the material. I will distribute this, and the Chamber can determine whether it wishes to examine the witness on this. It bears evidence registration number 0619-8785 and there is a two-page document, and I brought a copy for the witness as well as for Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to give the documents to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't have a translated copy that I'm aware of. I'll look overnight to see if I can assist in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is nearly 1.15. Thank you. Yes, very quickly, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we just need an extract from this document. We have two pages from a book here. We have to know which book in question, when it was published, where. We know nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, what is the provenance of it, from which book is it? It's part of a book that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would need to ask Mr. Tomic because I can't read it', it's in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can tell us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I can see the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you have to be given a copy then. So?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an article on the history of the Chetnik Movement in Croatia. It deals with the programme of the Dinara Chetnik unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know from which book it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's from a series called [B/C/S spoken]. It's a kind of journal publishing work done by Yugoslav historians at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope this is enough for Dr. Seselj. Anyway, we'll look into it again tomorrow. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of January, 2008, at 8.30 a.m.
